newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico wants APEC to move faster on opening trade.
newsitem.headline: Mexico wants APEC to move faster on opening trade.

text.p: Mexico wants Asia-Pacific countries to move faster toward their goal of creating a huge new free trade area early in the next century, President Ernesto Zedillo said on Tuesday.

Zedillo, who leaves on Wednesday for an Asian tour that includes a summit of Pacific Rim leaders, told Reuters in an interview he hoped the trip would also help Asians get better acquainted with Mexico's advantages as a place to invest and trade.

Leaders attending the Nov. 24-25 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit will review progress toward their goal of creating what is potentially the world's biggest and richest free trade area stretching from New York to Beijing.
The group has agreed a deadline for regional free trade among the bloc's developed nations, such as Japan and the United States, by 2010 and its developing nations by 2020.
Zedillo said that APEC's strategy so far of asking individual members to come up with unilateral action plans for achieving the trade goal was original but unlikely to succeed.
"I anticipate that we will not get very far with this method," he said. "We have to commit ourselves to a more rigorous procedure and to a much more precise accord."
Mexico, he said, wanted trade liberalisation, and "would like to see a much clearer critical path on how to reach this goal."

Mexico is also negotiating free trade pacts with the European Union and the South American trade bloc Mercosur but Zedillo said prospects for demolishing trade barriers with Pacific Rim countries were brighter.

"I think that if we can achieve some fundamental points of consensus, we could advance very rapidly," he said. "There are very interesting possibilities (with Asia), whether through APEC or through bilateral relations."
As well as attending the APEC summit in Manila, Zedillo will also visit China, South Korea and Singapore -- all fast-growing economies his nation is keen to emulate.

"We need Mexico to be much better known," he said. "Mexico has enormous comparative advantages. Its geographical and strategic location, of course, its membership of various groups of countries with free trade ... I think Mexico could be a very interesting gate of entry to the rest of Central and South America."
Zedillo said Mexico's growth had lagged behind that of Southeast Asia's "tiger" economies in recent years mainly because of its lack of home-grown savings to invest in industry and infrastructure.

But recent Mexican reforms such as the introduction of private pensions, he added, "will give Mexico in a very short time a very similar perspective in terms of economic growth to what we have seen in Southeast Asia, but perhaps even better because of (our) natural resources and our geographic location."
